extracted.intended_audience: educated general public / readers of Popular Science Monthly; students of comparative physiology
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science explanatory account of respiration across plants and animals, describing physiological principles, relations to temperature and activity, morphological origins of respiratory organs, and the major modes (skin, gills, tracheae, lungs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of respiration (animal combustion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiration is an absorbing and excreting process, whereby oxygen is received and carbonic acid and water removed; it thus becomes a measure of the amount of combustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Waste matter from tissue decomposition is 'burned' to gaseous products which are easily carried away; the body's demand for oxygen supports its 'fires' and prevents clogging/poisoning by effete matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of respiration to temperature and activity (cold- vs warm-blooded)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'cold-blooded' animals respiration bears a direct proportion to the activity and the heat of the body; in 'warm-blooded' animals respiration is inversely proportionate to the external temperature and directly proportionate to activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cold-blooded animals increase respiration with external heating and nearly suspend it during hibernation; warm-blooded animals maintain constant body temperature by using food as fuel, causing seasonal/latitudinal differences in food needs and respiration rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological principle of respiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of respiration is in principle an interchange of gases between the fluids of the structure and the external medium, air or water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exchange is effected by the physical action known as osmosis; the principle is identical in all creatures (air-breathers and water-breathers) and applies to plants that have true respiration; question remains whether 'vital influence' plays a part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration in plants vs animals (leaf respiration vs true respiration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaf-'respiration' of plants is a nutritive, deoxidizing process (separating components of carbonic acid under sunlight and depositing carbon), whereas true respiration is an oxidizing process (production of carbonic acid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During germination, flowering, or in darkness decomposition within the plant results in production and elimination of carbonic acid (true respiration); plants may have slight constant decomposition masked by nutritive processes—leaves function more like a stomach than lungs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological origin of respiratory organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiratory organs are fundamentally a modification or development of the skin; they may be developed primarily from the skin itself or secondarily from the alimentary canal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiologically all breathing-organs are expansions of surface for more rapid aeration of circulating fluids; because of this, organs vary exceedingly in form, structure, and position across animal groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of respiration modes (morphological table)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiration may be effected by: special organs developed from the food-tract (e.g., gills), general surfaces of the body without important modification (skin), or the entire substance of the body (respiration without special organs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table indicates relative importance (alphabetical small letters) for different groups; except in vertebrates no distinction is paid to air vs water breathing—classification is morphological not strictly functional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration by unmodified skin and food-tract
rubrics_metrics.description: Many soft-skinned animals respire mainly or entirely by the skin (e.g., amoeba, leech, earth-worm); the food-canal may also serve as a respiratory surface (e.g., polyp, jelly-fish, some annelids with water currents through intestine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amoeba has no permanent skin/organs and breathes without special organs; amphibians (some frogs, hellbender) use skin extensively; some fishes swallow air that passes through stomach/intestine for respiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic special organs of the skin (branchiae/gills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aquatic invertebrates often possess branchial respiration: gills (branchiae) developed from the skin as external or internal foldings where blood is exposed to water for oxygenation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Branchiae show great variety in position and form; many groups have accessory apparatus (cilia) to produce/maintain water flow over gills; crustaceans may attach gills to appendages or enclose them in cavities with mechanisms to renew water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ciliary renewal and gill mechanics (lamellibranch example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many gill-bearing mollusks renew water over gills by countless cilia covering filaments; powerful and rapid ciliary currents both renew respiratory fluid and aid feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ciliary action is so energetic that isolated gill fragments can swim via ciliary movement; bivalves often have siphons and valves to manage inhalant/exhalant currents and to keep gills clean using combs/brushes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial organs of the skin (terrestrial adaptations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special skin-derived organs adapted to air-breathing occur in articulates and mollusks (e.g., foliaceous gills functioning as lungs in land-crabs; lung-like sacs of air-breathing snails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terrestrial forms keep respiratory surfaces moist (small openings, secretions, or carried water) to prevent desiccation; some crustacean gills become functionally lungs despite being structurally gills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insect tracheal system and spiracle adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: Insects possess an extensive tracheal tube-system (tracheae) that bathes every part of the body with air; openings (spiracles/stigmata) are located on thorax and abdomen and can be opened/closed and protected by hairs, gratings, or membranes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracheae are prevented from collapsing by a spiral elastic thread; ventilation is produced by abdominal bellows-action (telescoping segments); adaptations include tracheal air-sacs for flight, spiracle protections to exclude water/dust, and larval/pupal modifications for aquatic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aquatic insects and air-storage strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many aquatic insect larvae and adults carry air into water by tubes, hairs, or by holding air under wings or legs; some larvae (mosquito) use a respiratory tube crowned with bristles to seize a drop of air at the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms allow air-breathing larvae to live in water; some species have very long tubes; others use posterior spiracles at waterline; adult divers may trap silvery air films under hairs for buoyancy and breathing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molluscan lung and facultative switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain mollusks (true snails) have a lung-like sac lined with blood-capillaries; some species (Lymnae) can switch from water-breathing to air-breathing, and Ampullaria have a divided sac allowing alternate breathing of air and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lung or sac has an orifice that can be closed by muscle; facultative switching demonstrates the underlying similarity of air and water respiration principles.
